# A uniform continuous-kernel inequality in every dimension

## Theorem

Let d>=2 be an integer and put theta=d/(d+1). For every v in [0,1],

    (1+v)^(d+1)/(1+theta v)^d
       +(1-v)^(d+1)/(1-theta v)^d
       >=2+theta v^2.                                  (1)

In fact the following stronger quantitative estimate holds:

    (1+v)^(d+1)/(1+theta v)^d
       +(1-v)^(d+1)/(1-theta v)^d
       >=2+theta v^2+(theta/4)v^4.                      (2)

Equality in (1) holds exactly at v=0. All denominators are positive,
including v=1, since 0<theta<1. The numerator (1-v)^(d+1) at v=1
is an ordinary zero power with positive integer exponent.

No mixed-integer OC theorem is assumed here. This is the explicit
scalar continuous-limit inequality arising in the shared-envelope
analysis of affine simplex chains. It does not assert any bound on
their discrete remainder.

## Lemma: a pointwise rational lower bound

Set

    c=(2d+1)/[3(d+1)],
    e=(d-1)/[6(d+1)]=c-1/2,
    f(z)=(1+z)^(d+1)/(1+theta z)^d,       z>=-1,
    g(z)=1+(1+theta)z+theta z^2/[2(1+cz+ez^2)].

Then f(z)>=g(z) for every z>=-1. Equality occurs exactly at z=-1
and z=0. This conclusion is uniform in the integer dimension d>=2.

### Proof of the lemma

Use x=1+z>=0 and define the two quadratic polynomials

    Q(x)=(d-1)x^2+2(d+2)x+3(d+1),
    R(x)=(d-1)(2d+1)x^2+2(d+2)(3d+1)x-(d-1)(2d+3).

Direct expansion gives

    1+cz+ez^2=Q(x)/[6(d+1)],
    f(z)=(d+1)^d x^(d+1)/(1+dx)^d,
    g(z)=x R(x)/[(d+1)Q(x)].                            (3)

All coefficients of Q are positive. Thus every denominator in (3)
is positive for x>=0. Introduce the polynomial

    P(x)=(d+1)^(d+1)x^d Q(x)-(1+dx)^d R(x).              (4)

Then the exact difference is

    f(z)-g(z)=xP(x)/[(d+1)Q(x)(1+dx)^d].                (5)

We prove P(x)>0 for x>0, x!=1, and P(1)=0 by Descartes' rule of
signs. We use its usual multiplicity-counting form: the number of
positive real roots of a nonzero real polynomial, counted with their
multiplicities, is at most the number of changes of sign in its
nonzero coefficient sequence. Zero coefficients are omitted from
that sequence. Reading the coefficients in increasing rather than
decreasing order does not change the number of sign changes.

First, x=1 is a root of P of multiplicity at least four. Here is a
direct verification that avoids an unproved polynomial divisibility
claim. At z=0,

    f(0)=1,       f'(0)=1+theta,
    f''(0)=theta,
    f'''(0)=-theta(2d+1)/(d+1)=-3theta c.                (6)

For example the second derivative has the explicit formula

    f''(z)=theta (1+z)^(d-1)/(1+theta z)^(d+2),

which also verifies the third derivative in (6). Expanding the
rational term of g at zero gives

    g(z)=1+(1+theta)z+(theta/2)z^2-(theta c/2)z^3+O(z^4).

Consequently f-g and its first three derivatives vanish at zero.
The denominator in (5) and the factor x are nonzero at x=1, so P
has a root there of multiplicity at least four.

Second, the entire coefficient sequence of P has at most four sign
changes. Put

    r_0=(d-1)(2d+3)>0,
    r_1=2(d+2)(3d+1)>0,
    r_2=(d-1)(2d+1)>0,

so R(x)=r_2x^2+r_1x-r_0. For a coefficient p_j of degree j<d,
the first term in (4) contributes nothing. Therefore

    p_j=r_0 binom(d,j)d^j
          -r_1 binom(d,j-1)d^(j-1)
          -r_2 binom(d,j-2)d^(j-2),                     (7)

where missing binomial terms are zero. On dividing by the positive
quantity binom(d,j)d^j, this becomes

    p_j/[binom(d,j)d^j]
       =r_0-(r_1/d) j/(d-j+1)
          -(r_2/d^2) j(j-1)/[(d-j+1)(d-j+2)].           (8)

For j=0,...,d-1 the first subtracted fraction is strictly increasing;
the second is nondecreasing. For j>=1 the latter is the product of
the two nonnegative increasing fractions j/(d-j+1) and
(j-1)/(d-j+2), and its j=0 value is zero. Thus (8) is strictly
decreasing, starting at the positive value r_0. The coefficients
p_0,...,p_(d-1), with any zeros omitted, consequently have at most
one sign change, and it can only be from positive to negative.

There are at most three further coefficients, of degrees d,d+1,d+2.
Appending three real numbers can add at most three sign changes.
The full polynomial (4) therefore has at most four sign changes.
It is nonzero, since P(0)=r_0>0.

Descartes' rule now shows that the root x=1 has multiplicity exactly
four and that P has no other positive real root. Since P(0)>0, the
polynomial is positive throughout (0,1). Its root at 1 has even
multiplicity, so its sign does not change there. It is therefore
also positive throughout (1,infinity). This proves P>=0 on [0,
infinity), with its sole zero there at 1. Equation (5) then gives
f>=g, with equality at x=1 and also x=0 because of the separate
factor x. These are exactly z=0 and z=-1, proving the lemma.

For an additional check, the leading coefficient of P is

    (d-1)[(d+1)^(d+1)-(2d+1)d^d]>0.

Its positivity also follows from the first two and one further
nonnegative binomial terms of (1+1/d)^(d+1). The sign argument above
already proves what is needed using the constant coefficient and
the even multiplicity.

## Proof of the theorem

Apply the lemma to z=v and z=-v, both in [-1,infinity). Let

    D(v)=(1+ev^2)^2-c^2v^2
         =(1+cv+ev^2)(1-cv+ev^2)>0.

The positivity also follows from (3), or directly from
1-c+e=1/2 and monotonicity of 1-cv+ev^2 on [0,1]. The linear terms
of g(v) and g(-v) cancel. A direct exact calculation gives

    g(v)+g(-v)-2-theta v^2
       =theta v^4 [1/4+e^2(1-v^2)]/D(v),               (9)

using the identity c^2=e+e^2+1/4, which follows from c=e+1/2.
In particular the right side is nonnegative, and strictly positive
for v>0. This already proves (1), with its claimed equality case.

To obtain (2), note that 0<e<1/6<1/4 and

    D(v)-1=v^2[(e-1/4)-e^2(1-v^2)]<=0

on [0,1]. Thus 0<D(v)<=1, while the numerator bracket in (9) is at
least 1/4. Substitution in (9) proves the stronger bound (2).

## Exact consequence for the normalized integral expression

For 0<v<=1 define

    A_d(v)=[f(v)+f(-v)-2]/(d v^2),

and set A_d(0)=1/(d+1), its limit as verified from (6). The theorem
gives the uniform explicit estimate

    A_d(v)>=(1+v^2/4)/(d+1)       (0<=v<=1).             (10)

This is a proved leading continuous-envelope inequality in every
integer dimension d>=2, with a quantitative positive gap away from
zero tilt. It does not remove any error term associated with a
finite arithmetic sampling of the affine leg.
